blocks.text: A missing value is honest about being a problem. It shows up as NaN, and every isna() check catches it immediately. An invalid value is not honest at all. It is present, it has a perfectly normal type, it passes every null check pandas can run, and it is still wrong. An age of negative 5 or an age of 300 is not missing, it is sitting right there in the column looking like ordinary data. That makes invalid values arguably more dangerous than missing ones, because they can silently pass through every check that only looks for nulls and quietly poison an average, a model, or a downstream report before anyone notices.
1. What Makes a Value Invalid

A value is invalid when it violates a domain constraint, some rule about what that column is allowed to represent in the real world, even though pandas has no idea and treats it as a perfectly ordinary number or string. Every column implicitly carries this kind of rule whether anyone ever wrote it down or not.

items: Age: a negative number, or a number like 300 that no human reaches
Percentage: a value over 100 in a column capped at 100
Birth date: a date that has not happened yet
Email: a string with no @ symbol at all
Phone number: digits mixed together with letters
Zip code: a value with the wrong number of digits for its format

blocks.text: None of these trip a null check. Pandas stores negative 5 as a perfectly normal int, an email missing its @ as a perfectly normal string, a phone number full of letters as a perfectly normal string. The value is fully present and syntactically fine as far as the dtype is concerned, and semantically nonsense at the same time.
2. Two Categories Worth Distinguishing: Out of Range and Malformed
Not every invalid value looks the same, and it helps to split them into two broad categories before deciding how to catch them, because the detection technique for one does not work for the other.
2.1 Out of Range Values

An out of range value is a numeric value that falls outside a plausible domain for that column. An age of 300 is out of range. An age of negative 5 is out of range. A percentage of 118 is out of range. These are numbers, they compare fine with less than and greater than, and finding them is a matter of defining the boundaries and filtering against them.
2.2 Malformed Values

A malformed value does not match the expected shape or pattern for that column, regardless of whether any numeric range is involved. An email without an @ symbol is malformed. A phone number with letters standing in for digits is malformed. A zip code with six characters where five are expected is malformed. These are usually strings, and comparing them with less than and greater than does not mean anything, so a different tool is needed, one built for matching a shape rather than a magnitude.

blocks.title: Why the split matters
blocks.content: Out of range values need numeric boundaries and comparison operators. Malformed values need a regular expression describing the correct shape. Treating a malformed value like an out of range problem, or the other way around, is a common way to write a detection check that quietly does nothing.

blocks.text: 3. Detecting Out of Range Values

The standard approach is to define an explicit valid range per column, based on domain knowledge rather than a guess, and then filter for anything outside it. An age column is a good example: nobody is younger than 0, and realistically nobody in a normal dataset is older than about 120.

The two conditions are combined with the bitwise or operator, not the word or, because pandas needs an elementwise comparison across the whole column rather than a single Python boolean. Every other numeric column gets the same treatment with its own boundaries: a percentage column would use (df['pct'] < 0) | (df['pct'] > 100), a quantity column would use whatever floor and ceiling actually make sense for it.
4. Detecting Malformed Values With Regular Expressions

For fields that follow a format rather than a numeric range, the equivalent tool is a regular expression tested with str.match() or str.contains(). str.match() checks whether the pattern matches starting at the beginning of the string, str.contains() checks whether the pattern appears anywhere in the string, and the choice between them depends on whether the format needs to control the whole value or just part of it.

code.content:
pattern = r'^[\w.-]+@[\w.-]+\.\w+$'
valid_email_mask = df['email'].str.match(pattern)
invalid_emails = df[~valid_email_mask]

blocks.text: The tilde negates the boolean mask, so invalid_emails ends up holding every row whose email did not match the pattern, including anything missing the @ symbol entirely. The same idea extends to any other formatted field, just with a different pattern.

code.content:
phone_pattern = r'^\d{10}$'
zip_pattern = r'^\d{5}$'
invalid_phones = df[~df['phone'].str.match(phone_pattern)]
invalid_zips = df[~df['zip_code'].str.match(zip_pattern)]

blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: Catching an Invalid Age and a Malformed Email
Consider a small customer dataset with two columns worth checking, age and email.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    'customer_id': [101, 102, 103, 104],
    'age': [34, -5, 999, 28],
    'email': ['sam@example.com', 'lee@example.com', 'priya@example.com', 'jordanexample.com']
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

blocks.text: Two problems are hiding in here on purpose. Customer 102 has an age of negative 5, customer 103 has an age of 999, and customer 104 has an email with no @ symbol at all. Running the range filter from section 3 against the age column catches both bad ages in a single pass.

code.content:
invalid_ages = df[(df['age'] < 0) | (df['age'] > 120)]
print(invalid_ages)

#    customer_id  age               email
# 1          102   -5    lee@example.com
# 2          103  999  priya@example.com

blocks.text: The email problem needs the regex check from section 4 instead, since neither negative 5 nor 999 style range logic applies to a string.

code.content:
pattern = r'^[\w.-]+@[\w.-]+\.\w+$'
invalid_emails = df[~df['email'].str.match(pattern)]
print(invalid_emails)

#    customer_id  age               email
# 3          104   28  jordanexample.com

blocks.text: Two completely different techniques, run independently, together cover the two categories from section 2. Neither check on its own would have caught both problems.
6. Fixing Invalid Values

Once invalid values are found, there is a range of fixes, and none of them is correct in every situation. The right one depends on how much of the row is still useful, how confident anyone is about what the real value should have been, and how many rows are affected.
6.1 Removing the Row

The simplest fix is to drop the row entirely with a boolean filter or df.drop(). This is appropriate when the row is otherwise unusable, or when invalid values are rare enough that losing a handful of rows does not meaningfully hurt the dataset. It is a poor choice when invalid values are common, since dropping aggressively can throw away a large chunk of otherwise good data.
6.2 Treating It as Missing

A second option is to overwrite the invalid value with NaN and then apply the same imputation techniques covered in the Handling Missing Values lesson, a median fill, a per column default, or a forward fill where that genuinely makes sense. This is appropriate when the rest of the row is still valuable and dropping it outright would waste good data sitting in the other columns.
6.3 Clipping to the Nearest Valid Boundary

clip() caps any value outside a boundary at the boundary itself, rather than removing or blanking it. This is the right call when the true value is probably just an extreme but plausible outlier rather than something truly impossible. An age of 130 might really be a slightly wrong but real elderly age, so capping it down to 120 preserves the row without pretending the age is unknown.

Clipping is a poor choice for a value like age 999, which is not a plausible outlier at all, it looks far more like a placeholder someone typed in for a missing entry. Treating 999 as missing, not clipping it down to 120, is almost certainly the better call there.
6.4 Correcting the Value

If the true value can genuinely be inferred, correcting it directly is the best fix, since it preserves real information instead of discarding or capping it. A common real world case is a misplaced decimal, a height column recording 1750 centimeters is almost certainly meant to be 175.0, and dividing by 10 recovers the intended value instead of treating the row as invalid.

blocks.text: 7. Validate the Rule Before You Trust It

Before any of this filtering gets applied, it is worth double checking that the business rule itself is correct, and that it is not accidentally flagging valid edge cases as invalid. A value of exactly 0 is the classic example. Zero years of tenure at a company someone joined today is completely legitimate. Zero as someone's age in a column tracking adult customers is almost certainly an error. The same number means two different things depending entirely on what the column represents, and no generic rule can tell the difference without domain knowledge.

blocks.title: Domain knowledge is not optional
blocks.content: A rule like age must be greater than 0 sounds obviously safe until it silently drops every newborn from a hospital records dataset. Always ask what the column means in this specific dataset before writing the boundary, rather than reusing a boundary that felt right somewhere else.

blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes
A few habits cause more damage than the invalid values themselves.

items: Treating every extreme value as invalid without first checking whether it is a legitimate edge case for this specific dataset.
Applying a fix like clip() or a drop immediately, without asking whether the invalid values are rare noise or a symptom of a deeper, systematic problem in how the data was collected.
Reusing a boundary or regex pattern from a different dataset without re-checking that it actually fits the new column's meaning.
Fixing invalid values before checking missing values first, which can hide how much of the row's other data is even trustworthy to begin with.

blocks.text: 9. Recap

items: An invalid value is present, typed, and passes every null check, which makes it easy to miss and arguably more dangerous than a plain NaN.
Split invalid values into two categories: out of range, caught with numeric boundaries and comparison operators, and malformed, caught with regular expressions via str.match() or str.contains().
Define valid ranges and formats using real domain knowledge for the specific dataset at hand, not a boundary copied from somewhere else.
Choose a fix based on how much of the row is still useful: remove the row, treat it as missing and impute, clip to a boundary, or correct it directly.
Before trusting any rule, check whether it is accidentally flagging a legitimate edge case, like an exact 0.
Investigate whether invalid values are rare noise or a sign of a systematic data collection bug before applying a fix on autopilot.
